scLimbsCoveredByACT: LIMB: 'the error is described to the user' — covered by ACT Expectation 2/3 and exercised heavily. Pass cases describe the cause ('Invalid value for age. Age must be at least 1.'); Failed Example 1 (3bb6b76) and Failed Example 2 (a51e05d) fail precisely because the message is generic/undescriptive ('Please fill the field correctly.', 'Invalid value for age.').

LIMB: 'the item that is in error is identified' — covered by ACT Expectation 1. Pass Example 1 identifies via aria-describedby->label; Failed Example 1 (3bb6b76) fails because the shared message does not identify which of two fields is in error; Failed Example 5 (d7863608) fails because identical labels in different fieldsets make the field un-identifiable.

Failed Example 3 (e76345a, display:none) and Failed Example 4 (ddcd6a3, aria-hidden=true) fail the 'visible'/'in accessibility tree' sub-limbs, exercising the requirement that the text must actually be perceivable (visible AND in the a11y tree).

varietyGaps: BIGGEST GAP: zero dynamic behavior. The SC is fundamentally a trigger-and-observe criterion ('if an input error is automatically detected'), yet 100% of cases are static pre-rendered DOM. Nothing submits, validates, or generates an error at runtime. The corpus tests only the rendered END-STATE of an error message, never the detection/announcement that the SC requires.
Single rule, single SC mapping (36b590 only), and heavy fixture reuse: 5 of 9 cases are minor variants of the same 'Age (years)' number field. Very low scenario diversity.

No ARIA live-region / role=alert / alertdialog / aria-invalid coverage despite three of the SC's sufficient ACT techniques (ARIA18/19/21) being exactly these. Programmatic/SR-announced error delivery is untested.
No native HTML constraint validation — an entire Understanding subsection — because no case uses a real submit button (all are type='button').

Content-domain monoculture: only generic age/name/address/color test forms. None of the SC's named real-world validations (state abbreviation, zip/postal code, future birth date, alpha-in-phone, bid-below-minimum) are represented.

Failure modes are narrow: the 5 failed cases cover only (a) message too generic, (b) field not identifiable, (c) hidden via display:none, (d) hidden via aria-hidden, (e) ambiguous duplicate labels. Missing: error present visually but with NO text at all (color/border-only), error on a different page, error that disappears on focus, multi-error scenarios where only the first is shown.

aspects.title: Error text is fluent and field-identifying but factually wrong for the value entered / constraint violated (boilerplate mismatch)
aspects.description: A page shows a non-empty, grammatically descriptive, field-identifying error message that satisfies rule 36b590's 'describes the cause or how to resolve it' check at the string level, but the described cause is factually wrong for the value the user actually entered or the constraint that was actually violated. The text reads as a competent error description in isolation, so it passes every programmatic facet of the rule, but it misidentifies the nature of the error and so defeats the SC's core intent that the user 'can determine what is wrong'. Examples: a phone field that says 'Remove letters and parentheses' against an all-digit value; a date-of-birth field that says 'Please use MM/DD/YYYY format' against a value that already IS in MM/DD/YYYY (the real, undescribed error is a future date); a password field that says 'must be at least 8 characters' against a 12-character value. Detecting this requires reading the field's stated constraints, the entered value, and the error text TOGETHER and judging semantic agreement — a contextual judgment no checker performs.
aspects.scLimb: 'the error is described to the user' / Intent: 'users ... can determine what is wrong' — the description must match the actual error, not merely be fluent.
aspects.whyUncovered: Rule 36b590 only asks whether at least one indicator describes the cause or fix as a self-contained string; it never compares the message against the actual invalid value or the field's real constraint. Every ACT pass case uses a message that is correct for the contrived value (Age=0 -> 'must be at least 1'), and every ACT fail case fails for a STRUCTURAL reason (generic text, hidden, ambiguous label), never for a message that is fluent-but-wrong. The corpus narrowness 'static hardcoded errors not from real validation' means a plausible message is never pitted against a mismatched value. No automated checker reads the value+constraint+message for semantic agreement.

references.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users are aware that an error has occurred and can determine what is wrong.
the user enters alphabetic characters or parentheses into their phone number field that only accepts numbers;

aspects.constructionStrategy: Self-contained pre-rendered post-error page. Render a labelled input with a retained value and a visible, descriptive, correctly associated (aria-describedby) error message. Make the message PASS every structural check — non-empty, names the field, states a cause/fix — but engineer a deliberate mismatch between (a) the value shown in the field, (b) the field's stated/native constraint, and (c) what the message claims went wrong. The judgment hook is: does the message correctly identify the actual defect of THIS value? Vary the mismatch type (cause that didn't occur, constraint already satisfied, wrong defect asserted) across pages. Include at least one foil where the message IS correct, so the aspect tests discrimination rather than a blanket 'all messages wrong' heuristic.
suggestedScenarios: Phone field instructed 'digits only', value='12025550143' (all digits), aria-describedby error reads 'Remove letters and parentheses from your phone number' — describes a cause that did not occur.
Date-of-birth field value='03/14/2027', visible error 'Please use the MM/DD/YYYY format' — value already conforms to that format; the real future-date error is never described.
Password field value of 12 visible bullets, error 'Password must be at least 8 characters' — constraint already satisfied; message is descriptive but inapplicable.
Email field value='ada@example.com' (valid syntax), error 'Email address must contain an @ symbol' — asserts a defect the value does not have.
Quantity field min=1 max=10, value='10', error 'Quantity must not exceed 10' — boundary value is valid yet flagged with a fluent message.
Control page: same phone field, value='(202) 555-0143', error 'Phone number must contain only digits' — message correctly matches the actual defect (should pass).
ZIP field value='9021', visible error 'ZIP code 90210 not found in our database' — error names a value the user never typed.

aspects.title: Post-submit page suppresses the error: form silently re-displayed (or shows a neutral/success banner) after a real validation failure — trigger-and-observe failure of NO indicator
aspects.description: The SC's most-emphasized procedural limb is trigger-and-observe: submit invalid input, then check whether an error is conveyed in text. The failure the Understanding calls out FIRST is re-displaying the form 'without providing any hint that the submission failed'. On a self-contained page this is staged as the post-submit STATE: the page representing 'the user submitted invalid input and the server bounced it' shows the form again with the bad value retained but NO error message — or worse, shows a neutral/green confirmation that does not mention the failure. A tool inspecting this page finds a form, finds no error indicator, and returns inapplicable/vacuous-pass (like ACT Passed Example 3), while a human who understands the page is the RESULT of a failed submission sees the violation. Distinguishing 'a benign blank form' from 'a post-failure page that suppressed the error' is a contextual judgment driven by page-state cues (retained bad value, submitted indicator, mismatched success banner).
aspects.scLimb: 'If an input error is automatically detected ...' (the trigger) and Intent: 'it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.'
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT page is the already-errored state with a hard-coded span; none represents a submission RESULT, and the 'no indicator -> vacuous pass' branch (Passed Example 3) is treated as legitimately passing. There is no case where the ABSENCE of an indicator is itself the failure because an error genuinely occurred. The corpus is 100% static with type='button', so it never submits, validates, or detects an error dynamically — the entire trigger-and-observe limb is unexercised. An automated checker cannot infer that a no-error page is the aftermath of a failed submission; only a human reading the page-state context can.

references.quote: In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.
This is a trigger-and-observe test — the tester must actively cause an error (submit invalid input) and then check whether the resulting error is conveyed in text. It is not a static inspection.
Attempt to submit the form and/or move to the next page. Determine whether the error is identified and described in text.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build the page as an unambiguous POST-SUBMIT state, not a fresh form. Encode page-state cues that signal a submission just happened and failed: the invalid value is retained in the field, there is a heading/URL/breadcrumb implying a result (e.g. 'Review your registration'), and there is NO error text anywhere. Variant A: form simply re-appears with bad data and no message. Variant B: a neutral or green 'Thank you / Your details have been received' banner sits above the retained-invalid form, contradicting the failure. The judgment hook: given this is the result of submitting invalid input, is the failure conveyed in text? Include a true-success control (valid data + success banner, legitimately no error) to test discrimination.
suggestedScenarios: Registration form re-displayed under heading 'Submission received'; Age field still shows '0' (below stated minimum 1), required Email still empty, no error text anywhere on the page.
Checkout page with a green 'Thank you — your order is being processed' banner above a card-number field that still shows an invalid 13-digit number; no error mentioned.
Login form re-displayed with the entered username retained and password cleared, page title 'Sign in', no message indicating the previous attempt failed.
Feedback form returned with the user's text intact and a neutral 'Form reset' note; the required Rating radio group is still empty and unflagged.
Survey page 2 of 2 shown after submit, but a required question from page 1 was left blank — the page advances silently with no error surfaced.
Control: same registration page after VALID input, showing 'Submission received' with empty cleared fields and legitimately no error (should pass).

aspects.title: Inline error message is visually placed next to the WRONG field, with no programmatic association to check
aspects.description: A self-contained page renders a descriptive error message physically below / next to a field, but the message's text refers to a DIFFERENT field than the one it visually sits under, and there is no aria-describedby tying it to any control (so no programmatic association exists to evaluate). A sighted user reads the message against the field it appears to annotate and is misled about which item is in error. Because identification by visual proximity ('errors inline ... next to the specific fields') is an explicitly sufficient method under the SC, the message passes every programmatic facet of 36b590 — non-empty, descriptive, visible, in the tree, identification 'through presentation'. The only way to detect the violation is to read the message text, read the label of the field it visually adjoins, and notice they disagree — a visual-spatial + semantic judgment.
aspects.scLimb: 'the item that is in error is identified' — identification via presentation/proximity must point at the field actually in error.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT Failed Example 5 fails only because two fields share IDENTICAL labels (a name-collision the rule reasons about via label text); it never tests a message whose text clearly names field A while being positioned next to field B. Rule 36b590 treats 'through presentation' (proximity) as a valid identification path but never builds a case where presentation actively points at the wrong target, and it has no spatial model of which field a message visually adjoins. The corpus narrowness 'contrived id failures no wrong field' explicitly excludes this. Automated checkers cannot judge visual adjacency vs. message semantics.

references.quote: it may be more appropriate to show errors inline, with error messages next to the specific fields that are in error
at least one of the form field error indicators allows the identification of the related test target, through text , or through non-text content , or through presentation
This SC requires that users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render multiple distinctly-labelled inputs stacked or in columns, each visually annotated by a nearby error span, but deliberately misalign: the span whose TEXT names field A is positioned in the visual slot belonging to field B. Crucially, attach NO aria-describedby (and no for/id error linkage) so there is no programmatic association for a rule to test — the only available cue is visual placement. Distinct labels (not identical) so the failure cannot be reduced to a label-collision. The judgment hook: which field does this message visually appear to annotate, and does its text match that field's label? Vary layout (stacked, two-column, off-by-one rows, side-by-side) to test spatial reasoning broadly.
suggestedScenarios: Stacked Name / Email / Phone inputs; the red message 'Please enter a valid email address' is rendered immediately under the Phone input; no aria-describedby anywhere.
Two-column form where 'First name is required' sits in the right column, visually aligned with the Last name field.
Field group with a small red span below each input, but the spans are off-by-one — each describes the field above it.
Card number / CVV / Expiry in a row; 'CVV must be 3 digits' floats under the Card number box.
Date and Time inputs side by side; 'Time must be in 24-hour format' appears under the Date picker.
Address form where 'State abbreviation is not valid' is positioned beside the City field rather than the State field.

aspects.title: Top-of-form error summary lists fields/causes/counts that do not correspond to the page's actually-flagged fields (summary-vs-state incoherence)
aspects.description: Following G83/G84/G85's 'text description at the top of the page', a self-contained page shows a top-of-form error summary block — descriptive, visible, in the tree — but the summary's CONTENT is inconsistent with the rest of the page: it lists a field that is not present, omits a field that is visibly flagged, states a count ('2 errors') that disagrees with the number of flagged fields, names a different field than the one displaying an inline error, or contains anchor links that point to the wrong control. Each individual statement may be a fluent error description (passing 36b590 at the message level), but the summary as a whole misidentifies the items in error, so the user cannot reliably 'determine what is wrong'. Judging this requires cross-referencing the summary list against the actual form fields and their flagged states — a holistic reconciliation no rule performs.
aspects.scLimb: 'the item that is in error is identified' applied to the summary method — the aggregate text-at-top description must agree with the page's actual error state.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT has exactly one top-of-form-list pass (Passed Example 2) where the summary is perfectly coherent, and one shared-message fail (Failed Example 1) that fails only for genericness. The corpus never builds a summary that is internally detailed yet INCONSISTENT with the flagged state — its narrowness 'single form one error pages no multi error summaries' captures that multi-error reconciliation is absent. 36b590 evaluates each indicator's describing text independently and has no notion of summary/field agreement. A checker can verify an anchor target exists but cannot judge whether the summary's claims match which fields are truly in error.

references.quote: indicates clearly in text at the top of the page that there were input errors. The text describes the nature of the error(s) and clearly indicates which field had the problem so the user can easily navigate to it
A single form field error indicator can be related to multiple test targets. For example, an error message at the top of a form can list all the form fields that are required and are empty.
provides a link to the field that had the problem so the user can easily navigate to it to fix the problem

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a multi-field form with a top-of-form summary block AND inline per-field flags, then engineer a deliberate divergence between the two layers. The summary statements should each be individually fluent (so they pass message-level checks), but the SET of fields/counts/links the summary names must disagree with the set of fields actually flagged (red border / inline message / aria-invalid) on the page. Vary the divergence type: phantom field, omitted field, wrong count, wrong field named, broken/wrong anchor target, or a field named that is disabled and could not have produced input. Include a coherent control summary so the aspect tests reconciliation, not 'summaries are bad'.
suggestedScenarios: Top summary '2 errors: Name is required; Email is invalid' but only the Phone field is visibly flagged red; Name and Email appear fine.
Summary lists 'City is required' but there is no City field anywhere on the form.
Summary states 'There is 1 error' while three fields display red borders and inline messages.
Summary with anchor links — 'Fix your email' with href='#phone' — the link target is the wrong control.
Summary names 'Password' as in error, but the only field with a visible inline error is 'Confirm password'.
Summary block present and descriptive, but the field it names ('Country') is disabled/greyed and could not have produced input.
Control: summary '2 errors: Email is invalid; Age must be at least 1' that exactly matches the two flagged fields (should pass).

aspects.title: Error is signalled ONLY by visual styling (red border / colour / icon glyph) with no error meaning in text anywhere on the page
aspects.description: A field is clearly flagged as in error by purely visual means — a red border, a red/yellow background, a red exclamation-triangle icon, a red CSS glyph, a reddened label with a trailing asterisk — but there is no text anywhere stating that an error occurred or what it is (no message string, no alt/aria-label conveying error, no visually-hidden text). The SC explicitly allows colour/icon IN ADDITION to text but forbids it as the SOLE indicator: 'The error must be indicated in text.' Detecting this requires a human to look at the rendered page, recognise that the ONLY conveyance of the error is visual styling, and confirm the error meaning is absent from text. A CSS-only red border or a decorative icon with empty alt typically does not register to tools as an 'error indicator' at all, so the page passes vacuously while a sighted user is plainly being signalled an error that is never stated in words.
aspects.scLimb: identification/description must be 'in text' — the SOLE-cue-is-visual prohibition: colour/image is acceptable only in addition to a text description.
aspects.whyUncovered: The entire ACT corpus delivers errors as plain text spans; there is NO case with an icon-only or colour-only indicator, and the narrowness 'no color only cue' confirms it. 36b590's Applicability is triggered by 'form field error indicators' and its expectations check the DESCRIBING text — a page whose only error signal is a red border may surface no textual indicator for the rule to evaluate, so it passes vacuously, masking the real violation. Automated colour-only detection (F81) is unreliable and cannot judge whether the field's error meaning is conveyed in text elsewhere; the rendered-vs-text reconciliation needs human visual judgment.

references.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.
it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.
the form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render a form in a post-error state where exactly one field is unmistakably flagged to a sighted user by visual styling alone, and verify NO text anywhere on the page conveys that an error occurred or what it is. Use a range of purely-visual mechanisms (CSS red border + tinted background, decorative SVG/icon-font glyph with empty or absent alt, reddened label + asterisk, yellow-highlighted fieldset) so the aspect is not a single CSS trick. Keep all visible field labels neutral. The judgment hook: is the error meaning available in text, or is styling the sole cue? Include a control where the same visual styling is accompanied by a proper text message (should pass) to test discrimination.
suggestedScenarios: Email input with a CSS red 2px border and a red-tinted background, value filled, no error text anywhere on the page.
Field with a red exclamation-triangle SVG icon beside it whose img has alt='' (decorative) and no nearby or hidden text.
Required field whose label is turned red with a trailing '*' as the only error signal; no message string anywhere.
Password field flagged only by a red key-icon CSS ::before glyph and a red outline; no words convey the error.
Radio group whose legend turns red in the flagged state, but no text says a selection is required.
Fieldset highlighted with a yellow background (the 'highlight in yellow' cue) but with the accompanying descriptive text omitted.
Control: same red-bordered email field WITH an adjacent text message 'Email address is not valid' (should pass).

aspects.title: Error is conveyed via an icon/image that HAS a text alternative, but the alt/name misstates, genericises, or mislocates the error
aspects.description: An error is delivered through an image/icon, which the SC permits provided the meaning is conveyed 'in text or a text alternative'. The page DOES give the icon a non-empty text alternative, so a tool finds the alt/aria-label present and is satisfied — but the alternative is wrong or uselessly generic relative to the actual error: an icon beside a malformed-email field has alt='error' or alt='red triangle' (describes appearance, not the error) or alt='This field is required' (wrong cause — the field was filled but mis-formatted), or two error icons share one generic title 'Invalid input' (cannot identify which field/what error), or the alt is the correct cause for a DIFFERENT field than the one it sits beside. The image exists, the alt exists, the role/name machinery is intact — only a human comparing the alternative's MEANING against the field's actual error state can tell the text alternative fails to identify or describe the error.
aspects.scLimb: 'in text or a text alternative' — when the indicator is non-text, the text alternative itself must identify and describe the actual error, not merely exist.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case uses an image as the error indicator at all, so the text-alternative delivery path the SC explicitly blesses is wholly unexercised, and the specific failure of an icon with present-but-misleading alt is impossible in a corpus of plain text spans. 36b590 would see a named non-text indicator and treat Expectation 1 (identification 'through non-text content') as satisfied, never judging whether the alt's semantics match the error. Automated checkers verify alt PRESENCE, not whether the alt correctly describes the field's actual error — that is a semantic comparison only a human (or judging model) can make.

references.quote: the only requirement is for errors  to be presented to users in text or a text alternative.
at least one of the form field error indicators allows the identification of the related test target, through text , or through non-text content , or through presentation
users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render a form where the error indicator is an icon/image (img, SVG with role=img, or icon-font) that DOES carry a non-empty text alternative (alt / aria-label / title), but the alternative's MEANING fails: it describes the picture not the error, names the wrong cause for the field's actual state, is too generic to identify which field/what error, or correctly describes a different field than the one it adjoins. Pair the icon with a field whose actual error state is unambiguous (e.g. malformed email, too-short password, out-of-range value) so the gap between alt and reality is judgeable. The judgment hook: does the text alternative actually identify and describe THIS field's error? Include a control icon with a correct, specific alt (should pass).
suggestedScenarios: Malformed-email field with an error icon img alt='error' — generic alt does not convey the email-format problem.
Filled-but-too-short password field with an icon alt='This field is required' — alt names the wrong cause.
Icon alt='red exclamation mark' beside an out-of-range field — alt describes the picture, not the error.
Two error icons on two different fields sharing one title attribute 'Invalid input' — too generic to identify which field or what error.
SVG role='img' aria-label='warning' beside a quantity field — name conveys severity but neither the cause nor which field.
Icon whose alt is the correct cause for a different field ('Date is in the past') placed next to the Email field.
Control: malformed-email field with icon alt='Email address is missing the @ symbol' (correct, specific — should pass).

pages.scenario: Telecom line-activation wizard, post-submit error state. Phone field is digits-only; the retained value is the all-digit string '12025550143'. The visible, aria-describedby-associated error reads 'Mobile number is invalid. Remove letters and parentheses from your phone number, then try again.' — describing a cause (letters/parentheses) that is factually absent from the value. The real defect (an 11-digit string for a 10-digit field) is never described.
pages.mechanism: Boilerplate mismatch: a fluent, field-identifying error asserts a cause that did not occur for THIS value. The value (all digits) does not exhibit the named defect (letters/parentheses), so the error misidentifies the nature of the error and the user cannot determine what is actually wrong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT 36b590 Expectation 2 is satisfied — a visible, in-tree indicator names the field and 'describes the cause or how to resolve it' as a self-contained string. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm label, resolved aria-describedby, contrast, textbox role. No checker reads the entered value ('12025550143'), compares it to the field's stated 'digits only' constraint, and judges that the message names a cause the value does not exhibit. That value-vs-message agreement is a contextual semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users are aware that an error has occurred and can determine what is wrong.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient intake, post-submit error state. Date-of-birth field retains '03/14/2027', which already conforms exactly to MM/DD/YYYY. The visible associated error reads 'Date of birth is invalid. Please use the MM/DD/YYYY format.' — naming a constraint that is already satisfied. The actual error (a birth date set in the future) is never described, so the only guidance is a no-op fix.
pages.mechanism: Boilerplate mismatch: message names an already-satisfied constraint (format) while the truly-violated constraint (date must be in the past for a DOB) goes undescribed. Following the stated fix re-enters the same well-formatted date and is rejected again.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes: a visible, field-identifying indicator describes 'how to resolve it' and is in the accessibility tree. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a labelled field, resolved describedby, fine contrast. citation.quote: An "input error" includes: information that is required by the web page but omitted by the user, or information that is provided by the user but that falls outside the required data format or allowed values.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit one-time-gift form; the donor entered 25000 (over the stated $10,000 online maximum) and the error is conveyed by a Material-Icons-style icon-font glyph whose aria-label is the literal ligature key "error_outline" — describing the picture, not the error.
pages.mechanism: The glyph exposes role=img name="error_outline" (CDP-confirmed), associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears a glyph identifier that conveys neither the cause (amount exceeds the $10,000 cap) nor that this concerns the amount field; it is an appearance/identity token, not an error description.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The element has role=img and a non-empty accessible name, so it is treated as a properly-labelled graphic — no empty-name or missing-role finding. Tools cannot know "error_outline" is an icon-set token rather than a meaningful description, nor that 25000 is out of range; distinguishing a describes-the-picture alternative from a describes-the-error one is semantic.

citation.quote: The "in text" portion of the success criterion underscores that it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.

pages.scenario: Homeware ecommerce checkout (en-GB); shipping postcode 9021 is too short and billing postcode SW1A 0AA! has an illegal character, but both reuse one SVG sprite and both <svg role=img> wrappers carry the identical hardcoded aria-label="Invalid input".
pages.mechanism: Both icons compute role=img name="Invalid input" (CDP-confirmed for both), each associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears the same generic phrase at two different fields with two different errors; nothing identifies which postcode or what is wrong (too short vs. illegal character), so the distinct errors are indistinguishable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each icon has role=img and a non-empty accessible name with valid aria associations — no unlabeled-graphic or empty-name finding. Tools have no notion that two correctly-labelled icons both saying "Invalid input" fail to distinguish two field errors; judging that the shared generic name cannot identify the field or describe the specific error requires human reasoning about context.

citation.quote: The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").

pages.scenario: Alumni reunion RSVP (en-GB); email ravi@@pembury.ac.uk (double @) and date 2024-07-18 (in the past) are both invalid, but a refactor cut-and-pasted the date row's error icon above the email row without updating it, so the email field sits beside an SVG whose aria-label="Date is in the past" — correct cause for the wrong field.
pages.mechanism: The email icon exposes role=img name="Date is in the past" (CDP-confirmed) via aria-describedby on the email input. The description is specific and well-formed but describes the date field's error, not the email's (double @) — it is actively misleading; meanwhile the genuinely-past date field has no surviving indicator and is silent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The icon has role=img, a non-empty (even descriptive) accessible name, and valid aria wiring — nothing for a linter to flag, and the alt is neither empty nor generic. No rule checks whether "Date is in the past" matches the email field it adjoins, nor that the date field lost its indicator; detecting a correctly-worded but mislocated alternative requires matching each alternative's meaning to its actual field.

citation.quote:
Determine whether the error is identified and described in text.
   - a. The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").

pages.scenario: Online-banking add-payee; the German IBAN DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 0X ends in an illegal X and is invalid (red border), but a Vue state-merge bug left the field's status SVG at its initial success state: a green check with <title>Looks good!</title> — an inverted text alternative.
pages.mechanism: The SVG exposes role=img name="Looks good!" from its <title> child (CDP-confirmed), associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user on the invalid IBAN hears a positive assertion that denies any error exists; the alternative does not identify or describe the error — it contradicts it, the worst form of the aspect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG has role=img and a non-empty accessible name from a valid <title>, contrast and aria wiring intact — no structural finding. Tools cannot validate the IBAN checksum, cannot know the field is invalid, and cannot detect that "Looks good!" contradicts the real state; catching an inverted/stale alternative requires comparing meaning against the actual error condition.

citation.quote: In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.

pages.scenario: CONTROL (passes): government heating-assistance application; the email carla.mendes#state.gov uses # instead of @ and the error icon carries a correct, specific alt="Email address must contain an @ symbol — for example, name@example.com", echoed by a linked error summary.
pages.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img with the full descriptive accessible name (CDP-confirmed) via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears the field identified and the actual error (missing @) described in a text alternative, with a matching summary — satisfying the SC's "in text or a text alternative" limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools would pass this page — but they would equally have passed the failing siblings, since they only check that the alt is PRESENT, never that it correctly describes the error. This control is statically near-identical to the failures (img + non-empty alt + aria wiring) yet is the only one a human marks conforming, proving the aspect is decided by the alternative's meaning, which checkers do not evaluate.

citation.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.

finalReport.title: Error Identification

problems: No genuine defects found in the case itself — it is well constructed. The only nuance worth noting: SC 3.3.1's *normative* text ('the item in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text') is technically satisfied at a structural level — the error IS identified and described in text. The failure is at the *intent* level ('can determine what is wrong') because the description names a wrong cause. This makes the 'failed' label correct but legitimately debatable as edge-of-SC; it is arguably also relevant to 3.3.3 Error Suggestion. The case is honest about this, framing it as the intent failing.
Citations vary slightly from a strict verbatim trace only by line-wrap whitespace (WCAG intent sentence spans lines 24-25); content is exact — not a defect.

Minor (non-blocking): the element-under-test selector #dob-err resolves to a

whose own AX accessible name is empty ({role:'paragraph', name:''}); the error text reaches AT correctly via the #dob textbox's aria-describedby description, not via the

as a named node. The selector is still defensible as the carrier of the mismatched message text, but the AT-perceived path is the textbox description.

Value 03/14/2027 is ~9 months in the future relative to today (2026-06-21), not literally '2 years' as the cited example phrases it — but the cited sentence is an illustrative WCAG example of the error CATEGORY (future birth date), not a literal threshold, so the mechanism still holds.

Doc factual inaccuracy: the .md and HTML comments repeatedly state the value is '12 characters' / '12 bullets', but the actual value 'riverstonelake' is 14 characters (AX value shows 14 bullets '••••••••••••••'; tabOrder reports input name 'riverstonelake'). The mechanism is unaffected (14 >= 8 still makes the length message inapplicable), but the stated count is wrong and should be corrected to 14.

SC-fit is arguable, not clear-cut: the error IS described in text and the field IS identified (aria-describedby resolves; AX description='Password must be at least 8 characters. Password requirements'; invalid=true), so ACT 36b590 / the literal 'described in text' bar of 3.3.1 is technically met. The failure is that the description names the WRONG cause — a borderline-3.3.3 / quality-of-description concern shoehorned into 3.3.1. It is a defensible reading of the cited 'nature of the error' sentence, but a strict ACT mapper could call it inapplicable to 3.3.1.

Masked value caveat: an AT user hears the value only as bullets, not the literal length, so they perceive the contradiction via the requirements checklist (length=met) vs the error line (length insufficient) rather than by counting characters. Contradiction is still perceivable, so the outcome holds.

Borderline SC mapping: the defect (an error message prescribing the wrong-locale format / asserting a false defect) arguably engages 3.3.3 Error Suggestion as much as 3.3.1 Error Identification. The wcag-understanding text itself notes 'Please provide a valid email in the format name@domain.com' passes BOTH 3.3.1 and 3.3.3, so a wrong-format exemplar is on the 3.3.3 boundary. The 'failed' label is defensible under 3.3.1 (the message misidentifies the nature of the problem and the user cannot determine what is actually wrong), but it is a judgment call, not a clean letter-of-the-rule failure.

The page asserts there is NO real error and that the validator is buggy (en-US lib rejecting valid de-DE input). The string 'Step 3 of 3' (cited in the selector/mechanism) lives ONLY in the <title>; the body stepper's current item is named just 'Review & buy' in the AX tree. No defect to report — this is a CONTROL case correctly labeled 'passed'. There is no accessibility error, by design; errorIsReal=false reflects the (correct) absence of any issue, not a defect in the case.

Minor labeling nuance: 3.3.1 here is arguably INAPPLICABLE (no input error was automatically detected) rather than strictly 'passed'. The ACT rule shape supports treating a no-error-detected success page as a pass/inapplicable; the doc's 'passed' is acceptable but 'inapplicable' would be the more precise ACT verdict. Not a blocker.

Citation-precision overreach: the .md pins the 'failed' verdict to ACT 36b590 Expectation 1 ('at least one of the form field error indicators allows the identification of the related test target ... through presentation'). The quote is VERBATIM (36b590.md line 51) and the WCAG Understanding quote is VERBATIM too. But 36b590 Exp.1 is the WRONG mechanism for THIS defect: 36b590 only checks whether an error indicator that EXISTS identifies its OWN related target and describes the cause. Here the indicators (red border on cc-number + adjacent message) DO identify their related target (Card number) and the message DOES describe a cause. By a literal 36b590 reading: Card-number has indicators that identify it -> Exp.1 satisfied for it; CVV has NO indicators -> falls into the 'has no form field error indicators' pass-branch. So 36b590 itself would NOT fail this page. The genuine failure is the 3.3.1-INTENT one captured by the WCAG Understanding quote ('the identity of the item in error'): the wrong field is flagged/named, misdirecting the user. The doc should lead with the WCAG-Understanding 3.3.1 basis, not 36b590 Exp.1.

Edge note on AT experience: for a screen-reader user the error span is loose StaticText with no aria-describedby (AX tree confirms it is a sibling generic/StaticText, not in any textbox's name/description), so the SR user gets NOTHING on any field -> that alone is a 3.3.1 failure independent of the placement trick. The doc's headline mechanism (proximity points at the wrong field) is primarily a SIGHTED-user harm; both harms are real but the doc frames it mainly via presentation/proximity.

Minor doc/page mismatch (cosmetic, not a defect): the .md persona describes a dynamic 'off-by-one loop' that emits the error into cell i+1 after a failed submit, but the .html is a static hard-coded snapshot with no JS. The rendered state is correct for testing; only the narrative implies runtime behavior that is not in the file.

The Trusted Tester quote in the .md ('The form field with the error is identified in text...') paraphrases the actual ref: the verbatim source bullet is '24a. The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").' The substance is faithful and supports the claim, and the primary WCAG citation is exact, so this is not a material defect.

PROMPT/METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): the prompt's 'Claimed scenario' describes a DIFFERENT page entirely — an Account 'Contact preferences' panel with Email/Mobile-phone inputs, CSS grid-template-areas, a 'phone-msg' grid-area mis-assignment, double-@ email value. NONE of that exists in case-03.html. grep for a-email-msg, grid-template-areas, grid-area, phone-msg, 'Contact preferences', 'Mobile phone' returns 0 hits. The actual page is an Aerolinks airline round-trip with two 'Travel date' legs (Outbound/Return) using flexbox, where a render-helper bug paints the return-leg error under the valid outbound leg.

Element-under-test selector '.a-email-msg' given in the prompt does NOT exist in the file; the inspect tool found no such element (dumped the whole AX tree). The real error element is 'fieldset:first-of-type .msg'. Any downstream consumer keying on the prompt's selector would fail.

The prompt's 'Claimed mechanism' (DOM source-order adjacency correct, grid geometry diverges) is the wrong mechanism for this file. The real file has NO grid; its mechanism is (a) duplicate identical labels 'Travel date' across two fieldsets defeating identification-through-text, plus (b) the lone error + red .flagged border rendered under the VALID leg defeating identification-through-presentation.

Minor ambiguity (does not invalidate the case): 36b590 Expectation 1 also allows identification 'through text', and the message text literally contains the field name ('الرمز البريدي' / postal code). A strict reader could argue text identifies the field, weakening a pure presentation-based fail. On balance the rendered presentation actively MISidentifies (message sits under City), which is the intended human-judgment call, so 'failed' remains the correct and defensible label.

This is a PASSED boundary case by design — there is intentionally NO accessibility defect, so errorIsReal=false reflects 'no defect exists' (as intended), NOT a flaw in the case. expectedOutcomeCorrect=true because the documented 'passed' label is correct.
Minor doc nuance: the .md/.html narrative emphasizes the discriminator vs. failing siblings, which is appropriate; the value here is corpus-discriminator coverage, not a detectable failure.

Meta-leakage: the .audit div (lines 82-93) renders, in-page, an explicit explanation of why the page fails and why automated checkers miss it ('Why automated checkers pass this page... the summary claims 2 errors in Full name and Email... while the one field actually in error (Telephone) is never listed'). This bakes the intended verdict into the page's visible/AX text (confirmed present in the AX tree as StaticText nodes), which could leak the answer to any judge that reads page content. Consider stripping it for a clean adversarial corpus. Does NOT affect correctness of the issue or outcome.

G83 citation is a loose semantic fit: G83 (verified verbatim at wcag-techniques/general/G83.html line 11) is about OMITTED mandatory fields, while this case is about invalid-VALUE errors (bad date / short mobile / bad postcode). The quoted principle (top description must identify which fields are in error) transfers, and the .md's secondary Understanding 3.3.1 intent citation (also verbatim, error-identification.html lines 24-25 and the 'identity of the item in error' clause at line 29) supports the mechanism precisely, so this is a minor citation-fit nit, not a hallucination.

Minor: Chromium's getFullAXTree serialization in inspect.js did not surface the aria-invalid='true' attributes as an 'invalid' AX property on the three textboxes (the 7 'invalid' string matches are the .field-invalid-class StaticText echoes of the page's own prose). This is a CDP property-filter nuance, not a page defect; the HTML source (lines 59,66,81) and the computed red 2px borders on exactly #dob/#mobile/#postcode confirm the real error state.

Minor (not a defect): the .md Citation section's first block stitches the 'An input error includes:' lead-in to both list items, which is a faithful paraphrase rather than a contiguous verbatim quote; however the element-level claimed citation quotes ONLY line 35 ('information that is required by the web page but omitted by the user, or'), which is an EXACT verbatim match in wcag-understanding/error-identification.html. No correctness impact.

Borderline scope tension (resolved in favor of 'failed'): one could argue 3.3.1 is satisfied once ANY error is identified in text and that fix-impossibility is a 3.3.3 concern; but understanding line 29 scopes 3.3.1 to 'the identity of the item in error', and a FALSE/incoherent identification (naming a non-erroneous, disabled, non-submitted control as in error) is a defect of identification — so the 'failed' label holds.

None. This is a correctly-constructed PASSING negative control, not a defect case. There is no accessibility issue, which is intentional and correct for a control. errorIsReal=false reflects that there is no error claimed (expected outcome is 'passed'), and expectedOutcomeCorrect=true reflects that the page genuinely passes SC 3.3.1.

Minor non-blocking note: each summary link's text omits the trailing period present in the corresponding inline .msg (e.g. summary 'name@example.com' vs inline 'name@example.com.'). This is semantically identical and does not affect reconciliation or the outcome.

PROMPT/FILE METADATA MISMATCH (not a page defect): The task prompt's claimed scenario describes a 'Community allotment newsletter signup', an email field with value 'tom@', and selector 'input#email.flagged' — none of which exist in the actual file. The real page is a Riverside Adult Learning course-enrolment form whose flagged field is 'input#seats.flagged' (value '6', 'Number of places to reserve'). Running inspect.js with the prompt's selector input#email.flagged matches nothing. The underlying SC 3.3.1 mechanism, however, is identical to what the prompt describes, so the page itself is sound; the prompt's scenario/selector/citation-snippet appear copied from a different sibling case.

Citation snippet in the PROMPT ('The error must be indicated in text.') is genuine, but the prompt attributes the file as the .md and quotes the .md's framing; the .md itself attributes the quote to wcag-understanding/error-identification.html. I verified BOTH .md citations verbatim in wcag-understanding/error-identification.html (line 24-28 for 'it is not sufficient to only re-display the form...The error must be indicated in text.' and line 130-131 for 'This success criterion does not mean that color or text styles cannot be used...identified using text.'). Citations are accurate and support the mechanism.

Minor citation-scope stretch: the second quote (F81) is verbatim in wcag-techniques/failures/F81.html but F81 is a Failure of SC 1.4.1 (color-only identification), not SC 3.3.1. It is used here as supporting context (F81's own note does cross-reference 3.3.1), and the PRIMARY citation (Understanding 3.3.1, lines 66-67) is verbatim and squarely on point, so this does not undermine the verdict — but a reviewer should note the page cites a 1.4.1 failure technique to justify a 3.3.1 finding.

F81's central failure condition ('marked with color differences only') is technically about COLOR, whereas the actual defect here is a SHAPE/glyph icon stripped from the AX tree via alt=''; the F81 framing slightly mismatches the real mechanism (the issue is not that color alone is used, but that the icon's text alternative is empty). The 3.3.1 'error not in text' framing in the primary citation is the accurate one.

PROMPT/orchestration metadata is entirely mismatched to the actual files: the prompt describes a conference call-for-papers form with a CSS ::after asterisk on label.flagged[for="title"], but the real page (case-03.html) is a car-insurance quote form whose error cue is a CSS background-image SVG glyph + red border on input#postcode.flagged. The prompt's 'claimed citation' (G84 asterisk-on-label sentence) also does not match the MD's actual citations. Judged the real files, not the stale prompt metadata. This is an orchestration defect, not a page defect.

Minor: the actual page's failure mechanism (background-image glyph) is arguably even stronger/cleaner than the G84 quote's literal examples (asterisk / red label), but the G84 principle 'a text description of the problem should be provided' applies directly, so the citation is still apt.

Minor citation hygiene (not a defect): the second .md quote (md lines 65-68) stitches 'to identify an error and provide error information to the user' to 'This type of programmatic information is not required for this success criterion' across an elided example sentence (understanding-doc lines 61-62). The elision IS marked with an ellipsis and each fragment is individually verbatim, so it is acceptable, but reviewers should note it is a non-adjacent join.

Minor mechanism framing: the doc/scenario leans on aria-invalid='true' as part of 'identifying' the error, but strict 3.3.1 conformance rests on the in-text description ('Email address is not valid.') being programmatically associated via aria-describedby; aria-invalid is a 4.1.2 (Name/Role/Value) state, not what satisfies 3.3.1. Does not change the passed verdict.

Second citation is a truncated fragment of the source sentence (source: 'For instance, "Email is not valid" would pass 3.3.1, but...'); the quoted portion is verbatim and correctly attributed, but it is a partial sentence quote.

No genuine defects found — the case is sound. Minor note (not a defect): the icon's name and the field's description resolve to the SAME token ('error_outline'). AX tree confirms input#amount (backendNodeId 20) has description='error_outline' via aria-describedby, and the icon (backendNodeId 22) has name='error_outline'. This consistently reinforces the claimed mechanism rather than contradicting it.

Minor doc imprecision (does NOT change the verdict): the .md/HTML comment claim the screen reader hears each icon's accessible NAME announced ('Postcode, invalid, Invalid input'). In Chromium the aria-label='Invalid input' actually surfaces as the DESCRIPTION of each textbox via aria-describedby (AX tree: both textboxes show desc="Invalid input" invalid="true"), while the two <svg role=img> nodes appear as separate image nodes with name='Invalid input'. The AT-perceived result the doc claims (identical generic 'Invalid input' heard at both invalid Postcode fields) is exactly what happens, so the failing outcome stands.

Fixture is a pre-rendered/baked error state (novalidate, action=#, no JS) rather than a live trigger-and-observe state. The cited trusted-tester test is explicitly trigger-and-observe ('Intentionally violate... Attempt to submit... Determine whether the error is identified and described in text'). This is a corpus convention (errors baked in); the resulting state is the correct thing to evaluate, but reviewers relying strictly on the TT 'must actively cause an error' note should be aware the page does not perform runtime detection.

Static page with NO automatic error detection: fields ship pre-rendered with aria-invalid='true'/class='bad' and there is zero JS (the only 'script/onsubmit' grep hits are inside the HTML comment). The cited reference refs/trusted-tester/sc-3.3.1-error-identification.md is EXPLICIT (lines 13,17,30-32) that Test 5.F is 'trigger-and-observe' and is DNA (Does Not Apply) if there is no automatic input error detection. The page relies on the corpus convention of depicting the post-detection error state; this is a legitimate convention but is in real tension with the cited reference's own DNA/trigger framing. Not disqualifying, but should be acknowledged.

The .md doc's SECONDARY citation (line 30-31): '"in cases where this is not already made obvious by the nature of the form." — wcag-understanding/error-identification.html' could NOT be located anywhere under refs/ (no wcag-understanding error-identification file exists; grep for the quoted phrase returns nothing). The prompt's PRIMARY claimed citation (trusted-tester, lines 23-24) IS verbatim and does support the claim, so the outcome label stands, but the md's unverifiable second quote is a minor documentation defect.
Invalid/non-standard <h0> element used in the header (lines 12 & 31). Renders as plain StaticText (AX tree bid=36, not a heading), harmless to the 3.3.1 mechanism, but sloppy authoring.

Minor narrative overstatement (not a defect that changes the verdict): the .md claims the SR user is 'never told an error exists' and may hear only 'Looks good!'. The AX tree shows the IBAN textbox does compute invalid:"true", so AT DOES surface an 'invalid' state alongside the contradictory description:"Looks good!". The real barrier is thus 'contradictory/misleading text alternative', which is arguably even more dangerous, but the absolute framing of total silence is slightly inaccurate.

Theoretical detectability footnote: the abstract pairing aria-invalid=true + aria-describedby pointing to a name 'Looks good!' is a contradiction a bespoke heuristic could in principle flag; however no shipping automated checker (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse/IBM) does this, and the core 'wrong-state success text' defect is genuinely semantic, so human judgment is required.

Minor doc imprecision (not a defect): the .md/scenario says the icon exposes its full name 'via aria-describedby'. Actually the icon's accessible name comes from its own alt (line 72); aria-describedby on input#email (line 69) separately pipes that same text into the input's AX 'description'. Net AT experience the doc describes is correct, but the attribution is slightly loose.
Cosmetic: doc says role=img; Chromium AX reports role 'image' (semantically equivalent internal naming), not a real discrepancy.
